analysis.one_liner: Creates federal consumer protections for income share agreements, which let students pay for school as a share of future income.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan group of four senators introduced the bill, but it never left the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: An income share agreement (ISA) is a way to pay for school where a provider fronts the money and the student later pays a fixed share of their income — more if they earn more, nothing if they earn little. ISAs today sit in a legal gray zone with few of the protections that apply to loans. This bill would write ISA rules into law: cap payments at 20% of income, require clear disclosures comparing ISAs to loans, let ISAs be wiped out in bankruptcy like ordinary debt, and give funders special tax treatment so the market can grow.
analysis.who_benefits: Students who use or might use ISAs gain protections the product currently lacks: payments capped at 20% of income, no payments when income is below roughly 200% of the poverty line, at least 3 months of voluntary payment pauses for lower earners, obligations that end at death or total disability, and ISAs dischargeable in bankruptcy without the extreme 'undue hardship' standard that applies to student loans. ISA providers and their investors also benefit, because the bill gives ISAs a legal framework, exempts ISA funding from taxation, and clarifies their treatment under securities law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: ISA borrowers, and the ISA industry

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps total educational ISA payments at 20% of a student's future income and requires that, when income is low, monthly payments leave the recipient with at least 200% of the poverty line to live on [S3].

Educational ISAs would be excluded from the bankruptcy rule that makes most student loans dischargeable only in cases of 'undue hardship,' so ISA obligations could be discharged like ordinary debt [S3].
Obligations end upon death or total and permanent disability, and providers are barred from accelerating the full balance after a default [S3].

Providers must disclose how payments are calculated, maximum payment counts and duration, the income threshold below which no payments are due, and a comparison table showing what a typical federal or private loan would cost at income levels from $40,000 to $200,000 [S3].

ISAs would fall under existing consumer credit laws, including the Truth in Lending Act, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, the Military Lending Act, and the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would write implementing regulations and report on the market [S3].

analysis.who_pays: ISA providers and their investors bear the compliance costs and the limits on how much they can collect: the 20% income cap, payment pauses, bankruptcy discharge, and detailed disclosure requirements. Students who sign ISAs still pay a share of their income — potentially for up to 30 years — and because the bill counts ISA funds as 'other financial assistance' under federal aid formulas, students could see their need-based federal aid reduced when they use an ISA. Federal taxpayers forgo revenue from the bill's tax exemptions for ISA funders and recipients.
analysis.who_pays_short: ISA providers, ISA investors, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill's stated purpose is to 'support the growth' of ISA financing, and it gives ISA funders tax-exempt treatment of payments received and exempts ISAs from securities laws and investment company rules — favorable treatment for an industry whose product can cost students far more over time than a traditional loan [S3].
An educational ISA could run up to 240 monthly payments over as long as 360 months — 30 years of income-based payments, far longer than most student loans [S3].

Providers may rely on a student's self-certification when checking how many other ISAs the student already has, and may assign an estimated income — up to a 10% assumed increase — and bill on it if the student fails to submit documentation, though reconciliation rights are provided [S3].
The bill counts ISA amounts as 'other financial assistance' for federal student aid purposes, which reduces a student's remaining need and can shrink their federal grant and loan eligibility [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students who use ISAs, this is a genuine upgrade from today's gray zone: enforceable payment caps, bankruptcy rights, and honest comparison disclosures. But the bill is equally a legitimacy bill for the ISA industry — it gives funders favorable tax and securities treatment designed to grow the market, allows obligations to stretch 30 years, and pushes ISA costs into federal aid calculations. Whether it is net good for students depends on how the CFPB writes the rules and how aggressively providers price ISAs within the 20% cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2022, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Todd Young introduced the bill on July 19, 2022, joined by Sens. Warner, Rubio, and Coons [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was its only action [S5].
It had three cosponsors — two Democrats and one Republican [S4].
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Neither side. ISA borrowers are no better or worse off, and the industry did not get the federal framework it sought — though it also avoided new restrictions. The status quo of unregulated, gray-area ISAs simply continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody — the status quo simply continued

industries.industry: ISA providers (fintech education-finance firms and school-affiliated funds)
industries.note: The bill would give ISAs a legal framework, tax-exempt funding treatment, and securities-law clarity that help the industry grow, while capping payments at 20% of income, requiring detailed disclosures, and allowing bankruptcy discharge. It entrenches ISAs as a recognized channel for education financing even as it regulates them.

The bill exempts ISAs from securities laws and investment company rules and makes payments received by funders tax-exempt, making ISA portfolios easier to build and hold. Investors benefit at the cost of forgone federal tax revenue.

A regulated, bankruptcy-dischargeable ISA with mandatory loan-comparison disclosures would compete with private student loans, which lack comparable discharge rights and face similar disclosure rules. Lenders could lose market share if ISAs grow.

industries.industry: Credit reporting, collections, and consumer-finance compliance sectors
industries.note: The bill subjects ISAs to the Fair Credit Reporting Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and Electronic Fund Transfer Act, and requires CFPB regulations — new compliance work for providers and their service vendors, and clearer rules for borrowers.
